conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You're in the ICU because your blood sugar was extremely high and you're in diabetic ketoacidosis. Do you know what that means?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve been here before. It’s when my body starts breaking down fat because it doesn’t have enough insulin, right? I feel like I did last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your blood sugar was over 1100, your pH was very low, and you had high ketones. We’ve started you on an insulin drip and fluids. Do you know why this might have happened this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My glucose meter broke, so I couldn’t check my sugars. I was still taking my long-acting insulin, but I only took 4 units of Humalog with meals instead of adjusting it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Not adjusting your fast-acting insulin during illness can lead to DKA. You also had nausea and vomiting—did you think it was a stomach bug?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I felt sick for a few days. Stomach pain, throwing up. I thought it would pass, but it just got worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your labs and urine—no signs of infection. So it’s likely a viral illness combined with not taking enough insulin. We’re giving you IV fluids and potassium, and we’ll keep the insulin drip going until your levels stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My chest felt tight earlier—was that from the DKA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your EKG showed some ST depressions, and your troponin is slightly elevated. But since you don’t have blockages, we think it’s ‘demand ischemia’—your heart was under stress from the high sugars and dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a heart attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not a typical one. It’s more like your heart was working too hard. As your DKA improves, the strain should go down. We’ll keep monitoring your EKGs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. My kidneys—are they okay? Last time I had issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine was high at 2.4, but that’s likely from dehydration. We’ve stopped your lisinopril for now, and your levels are improving. We’ll restart it once you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been taking my blood pressure pills regularly either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help you get back on track. We’re also watching your potassium—it was very high earlier, so we gave you calcium gluconate to protect your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that shot. It made my face feel warm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. Your levels are coming down. We’ll keep adjusting your insulin and fluids overnight. Try to rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugar is coming down, and your acid levels are improving. The insulin drip is helping. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Nausea’s gone. Can I have some ice chips?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can have ice chips. We’re still holding food until your levels stabilize more. We’re also watching your white blood cell count—it was high but seems to be from the DKA, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been drinking—just trying to stay in my outpatient program.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. We’re giving you thiamine and vitamins just in case. Social work will help you reconnect with your program after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood gas shows your pH is improving—up to 7.33. That’s a big step. We’re going to try switching you to subcutaneous insulin soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no more IV insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll try, but sometimes the acid levels can rebound. If that happens, we might need to go back on the drip for a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll make sure to check my sugars more often when I get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We switched you to subcutaneous insulin, but your anion gap reopened. So we’ve restarted the insulin drip for now. It’s not uncommon—your body just needs more time to recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was doing so well. Is something wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this is part of the process. Your metabolism is still adjusting. We’ll keep the drip a little longer and try again tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your bicarb is up to 18 and your gap is closed. We’re switching you back to subcutaneous insulin. You’re also having some hypoglycemia, so we’re giving you IV dextrose until you can eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel shaky sometimes. Is that from low sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s a sign. We’re monitoring closely. Once you can keep food down, we’ll stop the IV sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your troponin peaked at 0.28 but is now coming down. EKGs are improving too. This supports that it was demand ischemia, not a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need a stent or anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ll continue aspirin and high-dose statin. You should follow up with cardiology for a stress test later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is now 0.7—better than your baseline. We’ve restarted lisinopril. Your blood pressure is a bit high, so we’re adding amlodipine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess I need to take my pills more regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re giving you a new glucose meter and strips so you can check your sugars. A diabetes educator will go over how to adjust your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count dropped to 2.9—mild leukopenia. It’s likely from the viral illness and your history. We’ll check it as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. It’s expected after DKA. Just avoid sick people and wash your hands.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Off IV fluids, eating normally, and your labs are stable. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my insulin? It’s different now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be on 15 units of glargine twice daily—down from 18—and continue the sliding scale. The educator will review it with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Lisinopril and amlodipine. We’ll adjust doses based on your readings. Check them daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge today. You’re on aspirin now too, for heart protection. Any questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to see a dentist? My teeth hurt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noted poor dentition. Please schedule a dental check-up. Other than that, follow up with your primary doctor, endocrinology, and cardiology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me through this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay on your insulin, check your sugars, and call if you’re sick or can’t keep food down. You’re going home with services to help with follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before you leave. Your vitals are stable, labs are good. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. I won’t let this happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Keep in touch with your care team. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m just signing your discharge papers. You officially discharged as of now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll head home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels. Remember to follow up in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick call to confirm—yes, your discharge is complete as of 8:05 AM.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself. You’ve made great progress.
